summary: Defines how to carry GSM Half Rate speech codec data in RTP packets. It allows several audio frames in one packet and describes redundancy methods that make the stream more robust against packet loss.

eli5.summary: Phone calls get chopped into tiny sound pieces. This describes how to pack pieces of one older mobile phone voice format into internet packets, with extra copies so a lost packet does not ruin the call.

subtitle: How to pack GSM Half Rate voice frames into RTP packets, with optional built-in redundancy against loss.

tldr.problem: The GSM Half Rate speech codec had no standard way to be carried in RTP, and voice over IP needs packets that can hold several frames and survive packet loss.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload starts with one-octet table-of-contents entries, one per frame, followed by 14-octet speech or SID frames (or empty No_Data frames). Previously sent frames can be repeated in later packets, and the max-red parameter bounds how far back.
tldr.outcome: It registers the media type audio/GSM-HR-08, which is deliberately not compatible with early draft formats from 1999 to 2000.

today: RFC 5993 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Naming
sections.content:
RFC 5993 specifies the payload format for putting GSM Half Rate (GSM-HR) speech into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). It supports several frames per payload and loss-robustness methods using redundancy.

It registers the media type audio/GSM-HR-08. The name carries the suffix on purpose: the format is not compatible with the one in early draft versions from 1999 to 2000 of what became RFC 3551, so a different name avoids conflict with that older format.
sections.eli5: It is a set of packing instructions for putting one kind of phone-voice sound into internet packets, with a new name so nobody mixes it up with an older, different packing.

sections.title: The GSM Half Rate Codec
sections.content:
GSM-HR is one of the speech codecs used in GSM mobile networks. It works on 20 ms frames of narrowband speech sampled at 8000 Hz, which is 160 samples per frame. Each frame is compressed into 112 bits, equivalent to 5.6 kbit/s.

A standard Voice Activity Detection function spots speech pauses, and during pauses speech frames are not transmitted. Instead, Silence Descriptor (SID) frames are sent at the end of a talkspurt and about every 480 ms during pauses, so the receiver can produce decent comfort noise. For transport over IP, 480 ms may be too sparse, so the RFC recommends that an encoder outside the GSM radio network, such as in a core-network media gateway, send SID frames every 160 ms.
sections.eli5: The codec turns every tiny slice of voice, just 20 thousandths of a second long, into a small bundle of numbers. When nobody is talking it only sends a rare note saying what the background hiss sounds like.

sections.title: Redundancy and Loss Protection
sections.content:
One payload can carry one or more GSM-HR frames, either full voice or SID, for a mono signal, and it can mark frames as No_Data to keep things in sync or to show unsent or lost frames.

Generic forward error correction (RFC 5109) and audio redundancy coding (RFC 2198) can be used with this payload. The RFC also adds an optional GSM-HR-specific redundancy scheme, which may cost less packetization overhead. Conceptually, earlier frames are bundled with new ones using a sliding window; in the RFC's example, each frame is sent once again in the next packet. It works only when both the original and redundant frames are GSM-HR; otherwise RFC 2198 is needed.

No signaling is strictly required, but a sender may use signaling to bound the buffering and delay it needs. The cost is bandwidth plus receiver delay while waiting for the redundant copy. The sender chooses how much redundancy to use based on feedback such as RTCP receiver reports, and it must avoid making congestion worse.
sections.eli5: It is like writing each sentence of a letter twice, in two envelopes. If one envelope is lost, the sentence still arrives, but you use more stamps.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
A frame lasts 20 ms and is 160 samples at 8000 Hz. A packet covers one or more contiguous 20 ms intervals, and packets MAY overlap in time to provide redundancy. A receiver MUST be prepared to receive any speech frame multiple times. A given frame MUST NOT be a speech frame in one packet and a SID or No_Data frame in another, and MUST NOT be encoded with different voicing modes in different packets.

The RTP timestamp is the sampling instant of the first sample of the first frame, and the timestamp clock SHALL be 8000 Hz. The marker bit SHALL be 1 when the first frame in the packet is the first frame of a talkspurt, and 0 otherwise. The payload type is bound dynamically, and its assignment is outside this document's scope.
sections.eli5: Each packet has a clock stamp saying where in the conversation its first sound belongs, and a flag that goes up when someone starts talking after a quiet moment.

sections.title: Payload Structure: ToC and Frames
sections.content:
The payload is a table of contents (ToC) followed by the frame data. Each ToC element is one octet and describes one frame, so the number of ToC elements equals the number of frames, including SID and No_Data frames. The timestamp for frame N in the payload is the RTP timestamp plus (N-1)*160, modulo 2^32.

A ToC element has an F bit (1 means more ToC elements follow, 0 marks the last), a 3-bit frame type FT, and four reserved bits that MUST be zero and MUST be ignored by receivers. Frame type 000 is a good speech frame, 010 is a good SID frame, 111 is No_Data, and the other values are reserved.

A speech frame is its 112 bits in 14 octets. A SID frame uses 33 bits of SID data in 14 octets, with the other 79 bits all set to 1. A No_Data frame has zero payload octets. Frames the GSM radio subsystem marks as bad speech, bad SID or No_Data are not sent in their own packets; inside a packet carrying more than one frame they are marked No_Data.

A receiver SHOULD discard a packet whose size does not match what its ToC indicates, because decoding from bad ToC data could badly degrade audio quality. A sender SHOULD send SID frames every 160 ms, that is every 8th frame, in silent periods.
sections.eli5: Think of a packing list at the top of a box: one line for each item inside, saying whether it is a voice piece, a quiet-noise note, or an empty slot. The receiver checks that the box weighs what the list says.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two bit-level examples. In the first, three consecutive speech frames are aggregated in one packet. The first 24 bits are three ToC elements; the first two have the follow bit set to 1 and the last has it at 0, all with type 000, followed by the 14-octet frames in order.

In the second, the middle frame is No_Data, for example because it was lost before the RTP source sent it. The middle ToC element has type 111 and no data follows for it, so only the first and third frames carry data.
sections.eli5: The first example is a box with three voice pieces. The second has an empty slot in the middle where a piece went missing, and the list says so honestly.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The media type is audio/GSM-HR-08. It has one format-specific parameter, max-red: the maximum time in milliseconds between a frame's first transmission and any redundant copy. Allowed values are integers from 0 (no redundancy will be used) to 65535. If omitted, there is no limit. The parameters ptime and maxptime are as in RFC 4566. The type is defined only for transfer via RTP.

In SDP, the RTP clock rate in a=rtpmap MUST be 8000 and the channel count MUST be 1 or omitted. Remaining parameters go in a=fmtp. In offer/answer use (RFC 3264), max-red is a stream property; the answerer MAY change it but is RECOMMENDED to keep the offer's limit. Senders are RECOMMENDED to always include it, using 0 when no redundancy will be used. In declarative SDP, a participant MUST follow the declared value, so receivers must be ready to buffer for that much redundancy.
sections.eli5: The max-red setting is a promise: 'I will only repeat a sound within this many thousandths of a second'. The listener then knows how long to wait.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
General RTP congestion considerations apply (RFC 3550, RFC 3551). Putting more frames in each payload cuts header overhead and packet count but increases delay and reduces robustness to loss. If FEC is used, the redundancy must be regulated so it does not itself cause congestion.

Security is as for RTP in general: confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity matter. The RFC recommends SRTP (RFC 3711) if suitable, and mentions IPsec and TLS as other options. It says the format does not show significant non-uniformity in receiver-side computational complexity, so it is unlikely to enable a denial-of-service attack through pathological data, and it contains no active content.
sections.eli5: Sending more repeats helps with lost packets but clogs the road. Locks on the packets, like SRTP, stop outsiders from listening in or swapping the voice.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: 1 means more ToC elements follow; 0 means this is the last.

fields.name: R R R R
fields.desc: Reserved; MUST be zero and ignored by the receiver.

items.label: Good SID
items.desc: 33 SID bits in 14 octets, other 79 bits set to 1.
